title: Babylon falls (Revelation 17–18)
hookLine: the merchants weep over a city that trafficked in bodies and souls

cards: A shipping manifest sits in the middle of Revelation eighteen, and it reads like one. Gold, silver, precious stones, pearls. Fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet.
Ivory, bronze, iron, marble. Cinnamon, incense, ointments, frankincense. Wine, oil, fine flour, wheat.
Cattle, sheep, horses, chariots. And at the very end, two more items of cargo. The merchants who traded it all stand at a distance, watching a great city burn, and weep.
The reason the text gives for their tears: nobody is buying their goods anymore. Today's word is that city's end.

teach.b: First, the city. In chapter seventeen Babylon is a woman in purple and scarlet, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints.

Babylon once carried the people of Jerusalem into exile, and in Revelation the name becomes a code. Some readers hear Rome, the city of seven hills; others hear any city or empire that grows rich by using people up.
Second, the cry: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen." Then the mourners: "Alas, alas that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come."
Kings, merchants, sailors: everyone who profited mourns. Third, the end of the list. The King James closes the cargo with "and slaves, and souls of men."
The Greek word behind slaves there is the word for bodies.

Bodies and human souls, listed after the horses and chariots as if they were the same kind of thing. Some readers hear that as the heart of the charge: Babylon put people on the inventory. Fourth, the call.

teach.h: COME OUT OF HER, MY PEOPLE.
teach.b: Before the fire, a voice from heaven: "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins." Christians have heard it as leaving a place, or as refusing its rules while still inside it.
Some readers say Babylon is never far: in the clothes, the phones, the food, wherever a price is low because someone, somewhere, was treated like cargo.

how: Some Christians read Revelation 18 as a call to look at how goods are made and traded, and churches and Christian groups run fair-trade stalls and campaigns against human trafficking.

games.q: you're a merchant who grew rich trading with the great city. now you watch it burn from a distance. what do you do?
o: rush in to save the people.
stand far off and weep for your lost trade.
celebrate that the city is gone.
games.why: the merchants stand afar off, weeping, because no one buys their goods anymore. the list of what they sold ends with human beings.

practice: Look at what's around you, your shirt, your coffee, the phone in your hand, pick one thing, and wonder without guilt whose hands touched it before yours.

Then choose one thing you'll buy this week, and decide to look for a version made by people who were paid and treated fairly. If you pray, pray for the people whose hands made your things; if not, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Babylon falls. In Revelation seventeen and eighteen, the great trading city collapses in one hour, and its cargo list ends with bodies and human souls.

orig.note: Greek: body. in Revelation 18:13 the plural, bodies, is the word the King James renders slaves.
